item.title: Dodgers Reportedly Among Teams Showing Interest In 2.42 ERA Free Agent Pitcher
item.description: Relief pitcher Jonathan Loaisiga The Los Angeles Dodgers could be targeting relievers this offseason, and according to MLB Network's Jon Morosi , they are among the teams interested in Jonathan Loáisiga. Loáisiga spent the first eight years of his career with the New York Yankees. He had a solid tenure, posting a 3.54 ERA in 193 games. However, he had a 4.25 ERA in 2025. He signed a one-year deal with the Arizona Diamondbacks and had a great bounce-back year. He had a 2.42 ERA in 67 games for the Snakes. He did a great job keeping the ball in the ballpark, giving up just three home runs after allowing seven homers in 2025 for the Yankees. Loáisiga would be a great addition to the Dodgers' bullpen, especially if they lose Blake Treinen, Alex Vesia and Kris Bubic. Bubic was a starter for the Kansas City Royals but was used out of the bullpen in Los Angeles. Loáisiga is a right-hander, so he could be a good replacement for Treinen. Loáisiga ranked in the 96th percentile for walk rate, 93rd percentile for chase rate, 95th percentile for ground ball rate and 92nd percentile for hard-hit rate. According to Morosi, there are five teams involved in his market right now. The Dodgers may have to beat out other suitors, but they can provide Loáisiga a chance to compete for a championship on a roster with plenty of superstars. Other teams may not be able to do the same. More MLB: Red Sox Reportedly Considering Cutting Ties With $60 Million Outfielder

item.title: Rams Week 10 injury report vs. Cardinals: Puka Nacua is on IR, so who will step up for LA?
item.description: Image Credit: David Brytus-Imagn Images Rams Week 10 injury report vs. Cardinals: Puka Nacua is on IR, so who will step up for LA? appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . The Los Angeles Rams enter their Week 10 matchup against the Arizona Cardinals facing a significant offensive adjustment. Puka Nacua is on injured reserve after suffering knee and toe injuries against Washington, leaving Matthew Stafford without the receiver who powered last Sunday’s passing attack. Nacua caught 14 passes for 150 yards and a touchdown in the Rams’ 20-13 victory, drawing 19 targets. Replacing that involvement will require more than promoting one receiver. With Davante Adams and Jordan Whittington also on IR, Los Angeles must redistribute opportunities across a depleted group. The encouraging news is Stafford’s availability. Despite appearing on the injury report with a right elbow issue, he practiced fully throughout the week and carries no game designation. The challenge now is finding reliable answers around him. Rebilas-Imagn Images Tyler Higbee stands out as the main weapon to build around in Nacua’s absence, particularly on intermediate routes and crucial possession downs. His experience with Stafford makes him a logical candidate for additional attention, although that projection should not be mistaken for an announced target distribution. Higbee’s own health briefly complicated that outlook. An illness kept him out Thursday before he returned for limited work Friday. He received no game designation, leaving him available for an offense that needs dependable receiving options. The tight end group’s other injuries make his role especially important. Terrance Ferguson is out with ankle and hamstring injuries, while Davis Allen is questionable with an oblique issue. Colby Parkinson offers another available option after progressing to full participation Friday despite injured ribs. Tutu Atwell can provide a different dimension outside. His ability to threaten downfield offers a way to discourage Arizona from crowding shorter routes. Stafford connected with him for a 40-yard gain against the Chargers in Week 8, demonstrating the explosive element available beyond the depleted starting group. Konata Mumpfield also has an opportunity to earn a larger share of the passing game. He already produced a 48-yard touchdown reception against Denver earlier this season, giving Los Angeles another receiver with evidence of big-play potential. Consistency, rather than one explosive catch, becomes the next requirement. CJ Daniels Jr., Xavier Smith and newly promoted Brennan Presley round out the available receiver group. item.title: Chargers’ Ladd McConkey gets official injury status for MNF vs. Ravens
item.description: Mark Konezny-Imagn Images Chargers’ Ladd McConkey gets official injury status for MNF vs. Ravens appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . The Los Angeles Chargers could be without one of their key receiving options when they visit the Baltimore Ravens on Monday night. Wide receiver Ladd McConkey has officially been listed as questionable because of a back injury , leaving his availability uncertain heading into the matchup. According to ESPN’s Adam Schefter, McConkey received the questionable designation on the Chargers’ latest injury report. The second-year receiver did not participate in Thursday or Friday’s practices as he continued dealing with the issue. McConkey’s back problems first became noticeable before Los Angeles’ Week 9 game. He was active for the matchup against the Houston Texans but did not take the field because of back spasms. His limited involvement during the team’s preparations for Baltimore adds another concern ahead of Monday’s kickoff. The Chargers will likely make a final decision closer to game time. McConkey’s status could remain uncertain until the team releases its inactive list, which typically comes around 90 minutes before kickoff. If he cannot play, or is available only in an emergency role, Quentin Johnston , Tre Harris and KeAndre Lambert-Smith could handle larger responsibilities in the passing game. Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) There is some positive news for Los Angeles, as Harris has been cleared from the injury report and is no longer carrying a game designation. His availability would give quarterback Justin Herbert another option if McConkey misses the contest. Ladd McConkey has recorded 17 receptions for 286 yards and one touchdown across six games this season. His absence would be a notable setback for the Chargers as they prepare for a difficult road test against Baltimore. Hammer appeared to be frustrated with the call. He got his right hand on the ball, bouncing it hard off the floor and high into the air. Four successful free throws ensued. I just made a simple mistake, and I seen the ball, so I slapped it just for the heck of it. But it wasn't nothing. I wasn't real mad or nothing like that. And I told coach that, but in the moment and me doing that, it doesn't show how I was feeling. "Making that mistake, I know I just got to bounce back from that and learn from that because I can't be letting my team down like that, especially in tough moments. It was a four-point possession right there, so I can't be doing that and giving the team free throws and free points. We can't be doing that. We've just got to make sure we [maintain] mental toughness and being able to move on to the next play. OK, he called the foul. Let's keep going now." On the surface, the penalty Hammer received from Ford seemed to be too harsh for smacking the ball. But Ford pointed out Hammer also picked up a technical earlier in the week during a 112-64 victory over Muskingum. There was a pattern by the player and a method to the first-year college head coach's madness. "He plays with emotion and passion, and I coach with emotion and passion," Ford said. "I'm probably going to lose my mind at times, too. But you can't get a technical foul in that juncture. He's had that issue, and I want to get that cleaned up, but I also don't want the kid beating himself up. "There are going to be some games with a lot more emotion than there was in there [against Tulane]. He's got to be able to channel that [emotion] because he's a smart kid." When teams essentially start over every season during an era of college sports shaped by name, image and likeness deals and the NCAA transfer portal, how is a coach supposed to establish a culture? Give Ford credit for trying, even though he took a risk as part of the big-picture mission. A transfer from the University of North Texas, Hammer compiled 11 points on 5-of-6 shooting from the field (0 of 1 on 3-pointers), six rebounds, two assists and two steals in 17 minutes off the bench. His motor is relentless, and Akron had firm control when he was in the game. Without Hammer, the Zips found themselves in jeopardy of losing for the first time at home since March 5, 2024. "With about five minutes to go, I started second-guessing myself, and the [assistant] coaches were in my ear [about benching Hammer], but I tried to stick to it," Ford conceded. This is how Ford complimented Hammer through actions, not words: The coach would not have gone through the trouble of making an example of the player during a game unless the coach had significant plans for the player this season. Hammer's elite level of energy and hustle is unmatched among Zips players since UA legend Enrique Freeman entered the NBA and NBA G League. In a span of 21 seconds in the first half, Hammer dived for a loose ball, almost inadvertently causing an official to wipe out near Akron's bench, and took a charge from Tulane forward Joah Chappelle. Hammer has Zips fan favorite and Mid-American Conference Sixth Man of the Year candidacy written all over him. "If I could get on NBA Live and craft a player, I'd want [one like Hammer]," Ford said. "[He] just plays hard. And I think if we can keep him out of foul trouble and keep him from some things like that [technical], he's a guy that could be a double-double guy. No doubt about it, and then he could be extremely efficient while he's doing it." Akron forward Halil "Chabi" Barre, who had five points and a game-high 10 rebounds, injected some humor into the situation when he was asked to describe what Hammer has brought to the Zips. "Technical fouls," Barre said with a smile, causing Hammer to laugh while sitting next to him. Barre continued, "He's probably one of the toughest guys on the team. He brings huge energy on both sides of the court and obviously rebounding." As Akron seeks its fourth consecutive MAC Tournament title, the team will need Hammer on the court to reach its potential this season. UA wears a gigantic target on its back, and showdowns against Kent State, Miami, Toledo, among others, are sure to be intense. If Hammer were better equipped to harness his competitive fire in those moments, he and Ford would be able to look back at Akron versus Tulane as a turning point. item.title: Brad Holmes Fires Back at Critics Over Detroit Lions Trade Deadline Decisions
item.description: Detroit Lions general manager Brad Holmes has heard the criticism about his approach to the NFL trade deadline, and he has a message for anyone who believes the team has become complacent. He’s not buying it. Not even a little bit. During an exclusive interview with Colton Pouncy of The Athletic , Holmes addressed concerns that Detroit failed to do enough to improve its roster before Tuesday’s deadline. While other NFC contenders made aggressive moves, the Lions added veteran safety Andre Cisco from the New York Jets and decided against making another major trade. That decision has sparked plenty of criticism , but Holmes made it clear that a lack of headline-grabbing transactions does not mean the organization isn’t working to get better. Whatever we did, it’s not indicative of our work ethic or complacency or our process. The trade deadline happens to have a title on it, but it’s really not any other different week besides — you might get an uptick in phone calls, but we’re calling and working the phones all year. Like, we’re doing this stuff in August and September, October. We’re doing this all the time, year-round. So, there’s no complacency. Nobody’s in position to be complacent. item.title: Michigan QB Bryce Underwood replaces Tommy Carr after difficult start vs. Oregon
item.description: Vincent Carchietta-Imagn Images Michigan QB Bryce Underwood replaces Tommy Carr after difficult start vs. Oregon appeared first on ClutchPoints . Add ClutchPoints as a Preferred Source by clicking here . Michigan football rolled with a new play-caller for Tommy Carr before facing the Oregon Ducks . But coach Kyle Whittingham pivoted back to Bryce Underwood Saturday. All because of Carr’s rough start post Jason Beck firing as offensive coordinator . Carr got pulled after posting these disastrous numbers: 1-of-5 for eight yards. Michigan needed to lean into the ground game to produce any kind of offense in Eugene. Watch sports LIVE with fuboTV (free trial) So running back Savion Hiter tallied 71 yards on just two carries. Jordan Marshall added 14 yards with two carries. But Oregon jumped on the Wolverines early with a 14-7 lead. Featuring Ducks quarterback Dylan Raiola exposing the Michigan secondary with a 60-yard touchdown lob to Jeremiah McClellan. Raiola added a shorter two-yarder that built the Ducks lead to 14-0. Hiter, though, sliced through the Oregon defense on a 70-yard scoring scamper that cut the deficit to 14-7. Michigan still has endured a tumultuous season in year one of the Whittingham era. The Wolverines started by escaping Western Michigan with an Underwood Hail Mary that involved a controversial play clock debate. Michigan later pulled Underwood from behind center amid some notable struggles on offense during the time Beck was calling the offense. Which swung the starting spot over to Carr. Carr gets pulled now amid his own slow start as “Whitt” turns back to Underwood. Michigan is aiming to install any kind of momentum. Especially after absorbing the brutal 15-6 loss to struggling Michigan State one week ago. Yet the Wolverines need just one victory to become bowl eligible at 5-4 overall. item.title: No. 6 Texas at No. 21 LSU live updates: Horns try to overcome travel issues
item.description: Nothing about this weekend was ever going to be easy — going into Death Valley and attempting to beat the supremely talented No. 21 LSU Tigers at night in the sixth conference game in six weeks for the No. 6 Texas Longhorns, who have already secured wins against four other ranked opponents. But Friday’s shocking FAA ground stop threw everything into chaos. Just as the Longhorns were set to depart Austin, the order forced Steve Sarkisian’s team to deplane and return to campus for a meal, walk-though, and meetings before the plane was finally able to depart seven hours late. By the time Texas got to its team hotel in Baton Rouge, it was past midnight. Now it’s up to a team that Sarkisian lauded for its undeniable toughness last week to turn that inconvenience into a historical footnote instead of an excuse. Able to keep their Saturday schedule, the Horns expect to perform well at Tiger Stadium, according to ESPN’s Holly Rowe. Here's an inside look to the struggled Texas had to deal with to get to Baton Rouge with the FAA ground stop pic.twitter.com/bUgIMeKlF1 — Nash (@NashTalksTexas) November 14, 2026 With a win, Texas has a 95-percent chance to return to the College Football Playoff . With a loss? Down to 60 percent. Those are the stakes on Saturday.

item.description: Dillon Duff has developed an effective working relationship with tight end Garrett Oakley (as well as wide receiver Jaron Tibbs). | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images A defensive struggle for the most part, marred by two Kansas State turnovers, led to yet another defeat for the visiting Wildcats as they fell 20-10 to the TCU Horned Frogs this afternoon at Amon Carter Stadium in Fort Worth, Texas. K-State (4-6, 1-6 Big 12) made some progress with their shaky run defense today, but a key fumble early in the game led to an early TCU (3-4, 5-5 Big 12) touchdown, and the Frogs shut down the Wildcat running game well enough to prevent the Cats from mounting an effective comeback. The Cats got to midfield before having to punt on the opening drive, then forced a 3-and-out. But Rodney Fields fumbled at the Wildcat 28 and TCU recovered; three plays later, Kari Ashley took a direct snap and raced 19 yards to put TCU on the board first. Both teams went 3-and-out, then the Cats managed one first down before punting; Jaden Craig then hit Jordan Dwyer for 41 yards into K-State territory. TCU had to settle for a 29-yard Kyle Lemmermann field goal as the defense managed to hold after that. K-State had to punt again, but on TCU’s drive sacks on first and third down by Kamari Burns and Jayden Bryant with Travis Bates forced yet another punt. Near midfield on 3rd-and-10, Duff’s inexperience led to another sack, and another punt, Simon McClannan’s fifth of the first half. As TCU drove, Darien Whitaker recorded the third Wildcat sack of the half, trapping TCU with a 3rd-and-15 at the 35; Burns and Bates combined for the fourth sack on the next play, pushing the Frogs back far enough to have to punt instead of attempting a field goal. But only 15 seconds remained in the half, and K-State just took a knee to reset. TCU drove well after the half, marching downfield and scoring on a 5-yard pass from Craig to Jacobe Hayes to make the score 17-0. On the ensuing drive, one 24-yard run by Joe Jackson nearly doubled the team’s entire rushing output on its own, getting K-State into TCU territory for the first time all afternoon. A 55-yard field goal by Luis Rodriguez — a career high — broke up the shutout. The Frogs got into Wildcat territory, but a pair of big stops inside the 40 left TCU in no-man’s land, and they had to punt. It wasn’t much of a gain, as the punt went into the end zone. Two plays later, Duff found Jaron Tibbs wide open for a 53-yard score to close the gap to 17-10. The defense gave ground, though, and the Frogs reached the red zone. But the Cats held there, forcing a 36-yard field goal by Lemmermann. A small victory, but it did make the game a two-score affair again. item.content:encoded: Dillon Duff has developed an effective working relationship with tight end Garrett Oakley (as well as wide receiver Jaron Tibbs). | Icon Sportswire via Getty Images A defensive struggle for the most part, marred by two Kansas State turnovers, led to yet another defeat for the visiting Wildcats as they fell 20-10 to the TCU Horned Frogs this afternoon at Amon Carter Stadium in Fort Worth, Texas. K-State (4-6, 1-6 Big 12) made some progress with their shaky run defense today, but a key fumble early in the game led to an early TCU (3-4, 5-5 Big 12) touchdown, and the Frogs shut down the Wildcat running game well enough to prevent the Cats from mounting an effective comeback. The Cats got to midfield before having to punt on the opening drive, then forced a 3-and-out. But Rodney Fields fumbled at the Wildcat 28 and TCU recovered; three plays later, Kari Ashley took a direct snap and raced 19 yards to put TCU on the board first. Both teams went 3-and-out, then the Cats managed one first down before punting; Jaden Craig then hit Jordan Dwyer for 41 yards into K-State territory. TCU had to settle for a 29-yard Kyle Lemmermann field goal as the defense managed to hold after that. K-State had to punt again, but on TCU’s drive sacks on first and third down by Kamari Burns and Jayden Bryant with Travis Bates forced yet another punt. Near midfield on 3rd-and-10, Duff’s inexperience led to another sack, and another punt, Simon McClannan’s fifth of the first half. As TCU drove, Darien Whitaker recorded the third Wildcat sack of the half, trapping TCU with a 3rd-and-15 at the 35; Burns and Bates combined for the fourth sack on the next play, pushing the Frogs back far enough to have to punt instead of attempting a field goal. But only 15 seconds remained in the half, and K-State just took a knee to reset. TCU drove well after the half, marching downfield and scoring on a 5-yard pass from Craig to Jacobe Hayes to make the score 17-0. On the ensuing drive, one 24-yard run by Joe Jackson nearly doubled the team’s entire rushing output on its own, getting K-State into TCU territory for the first time all afternoon. A 55-yard field goal by Luis Rodriguez — a career high — broke up the shutout. The Frogs got into Wildcat territory, but a pair of big stops inside the 40 left TCU in no-man’s land, and they had to punt. It wasn’t much of a gain, as the punt went into the end zone. Two plays later, Duff found Jaron Tibbs wide open for a 53-yard score to close the gap to 17-10. The defense gave ground, though, and the Frogs reached the red zone. But the Cats held there, forcing a 36-yard field goal by Lemmermann. A small victory, but it did make the game a two-score affair again. K-State moved the ball in response, but ended up having to punt. A quick 3-and-out got them the ball back again, but as the Cats marched toward the red zone, the offensive line got worked over, resulting in a 15-yard sack and a fumble by Duff, recovered near midfield with only 1:58 to play. TCU was able to kill the clock, and that was that. Duff was 22-33 for 244 yards with a touchdown and no interceptions. On the ground, he had 10 carries for a loss of seven yards and one fumble — but adjusted for sacks, that was actually 10 for 31. The Cats were terrible on the ground; Jackson (5 carries) and Fields (9) each had 33 yards. Tibbs and Garrett Oakley carried the weight in the air, Tibbs catching eight balls for 115 yards and a score, Oakley snagging six for 60. Derrick Salley had two catches for 32 yards, and Linkon Cure had two for 26. TCU outgained the Cats 324-302, outrushing K-State 99-58. The Wildcats did outgain the Frogs in the air 244-225. Penalties were a minor issue, K-State picking up four for 41 yards while TCU was only flagged once for ten. The Cats actually gained more yards per play, 5.2 to 4.7, but lost the turnover battle 2-0 and that may have ultimately been the deciding factor in the game. TCU led time of possession 32-28. WHAT WE… OBSERVED We didn’t learn much, because this team is irretrievably broken for the season thanks to injuries. But there were takeaways worth noting this week. 1) Whatever they did to work on run defense worked — today. TCU was held under 100 yards on the ground (although taking sack yardage into account it was 116 yards). Nearly half of that yardage came on a single play; subtract Payne’s 55-yard run and TCU was held to 61 yards otherwise. That’s worth noting, and good. (And four sacks? Gravy.) 2) Dillon Duff was the better quarterback in this game — indisputably. Duff wasn’t just the better of two bad quarterbacks, either. His passer rating on the day was 138.8, completing 2/3 of his passes, not making any egregious mistakes. He’s still shaky sometimes and runs himself into a sack, but he’s vastly improved over his first start, and showed progress over his relief appearance last week, in which he was also not bad at all. If he’s ultimately the future, he may have what it takes after all. 3) The offensive line, though. Oof. The line gave up five sacks today, which is almost 30% of the total allowed for the entire season . And they couldn’t run block to save their lives. It’s been an issue all year, off and on, especially in the eye test. Today, the numbers proved the hypothesis. PLAYERS OF THE GAME Have a hundred-yard day, be offensive player of the game, Jaron Tibbs . On defense, the four Wildcats who recorded full or partial sacks could’ve taken the honor, but Asa Newsom was everywhere today, recording 11 tackles, five solo, and was in on a tackle for loss. NEXT It doesn’t get any easier. #23 Arizona comes to town for the home finale, time and network yet to be determined.

item.title: Girona makes a comeback in Oviedo and takes three golden points
item.description: Girona makes a comeback in Oviedo and takes three golden points Girona turned the score around at the Carlos Tartiere and defeated Oviedo 1-2. After a goalless first half, but with Girona dominating — they had 65% possession — the match became much more lively in the second half. Oviedo took the lead in the 47th minute with a goal from Reina, but Girona did not give up. In the 59th minute, Abel Ruiz equalized with an assist from Pyshchur. Five minutes later, in the 64th minute, Pyshchur completed the comeback: a ball remained in the area, and the forward stretched his leg to push it into the back of the net, securing the final 1-2 score. The victory allows Girona to reach 24 points. The next match will be on Sunday at Montilivi, at 6:30 PM, against Eibar.

item.title: Panthers S Zakee Wheatley fined for play vs. Broncos in Week 9
item.description: Photo by Cooper Neill/Getty Images | Getty Images Panthers safety Zakee Wheatley has been fined $5,626 for a hit on a defenseless player in Carolina’s Week 9 loss to the Denver Broncos. The fine was assessed for a first-and-10 Broncos play with 19 seconds to play in the first quarter of Week 9. Marco Wilson was flagged for taunting on the same play, but Wheatley was not flagged at the time. It’s Wheatley’s second fine of the 2026 season. He was also fined $5,626 for taunting against the Philadelphia Eagles in Week 6. No Denver players were fined for any plays in the Panthers’ 26-21 loss in Week 9. The NFL divides up the money it collects from player fines between the NFLPA’s efforts to support retired players, the NFL Foundation, and other nonprofits supporting youth sports, community health initiatives, and player health and safety at all levels of sports. The Panthers will face off against the New Orleans Saints on the road in Week 11.

item.title: Grand Slam of Darts: Schedule, results & prize money
item.description: Luke Littler became world number one for the first time when he won the Grand Slam of Darts in 2025 [Press Association] The 2026 Grand Slam of Darts gets under way on Saturday, as another of the Professional Darts Corporation's (PDC) major titles is set to be won in Wolverhampton. This edition is bigger than ever, with 48 players taking part, and unlike most of darts' major tournaments, the players are split into groups in the initial phase, rather than a straight knockout format. Each player will face two opponents in their group, with only the group winner progressing into the last 16. The rest of the competition is a straight knockout format. Luke Littler is the defending champion following a 16-11 victory over Luke Humphries in the 2025 final to become world number one for the first time. Littler faces a tough start, with Beau Greaves his opponent on the opening evening, and Neils Zonneveld, who beat Littler in their only previous meeting, completing the group. When is the Grand Slam of Darts? The tournament lasts for nine days from Saturday, 14 November to Sunday, 22 November. Group stage (14-17 November) - 48 matches Second round (18-19 November) - eight matches Quarter-finals (20-21 November) Semi-finals (22 November) Final (22 November) What is the format? In the group stage, the format is best of nine legs, or first to five legs. In the initial phase, two points are awarded for a win, with the group winner progressing to the last 16. In case of players being level on points at the end of the group phase, the following tie-breakers apply: Total Leg Difference Total Legs Won Total Legs Won Against Throw Highest Total Tournament Average (to two decimal places) Highest Winning Match Average (to two decimal places) A play-off - nine-dart leg Second-round matches are a best-of-19 format, or first to 10 legs. The quarter-finals, semi-finals and final are best of 31 legs, or first to 16 legs. Who is playing and how did they qualify? With the tournament expanded, a new set of qualification rules have been put in place. Up to 24 players could qualify from reaching a major PDC televised final in the past 12 months, but only nine ended up qualifying via that route, partly because of the dominance Littler has shown. Ten players reached Wolverhampton from the PDC youth, development and challenge tours, the Women's Matchplay and Women's Series and championships from across the globe. Six more secured places through the European Tour, while 13 qualified with a Players Championship win. The final 10 spots, which include ninth seed Stephen Bunting, were claimed in a PDC tour card holder qualifying event. From there, the top-16 ranked players in the PDC's order of merit were seeded and filled pot one. The next 16 went into pot two and the final 16 made up pot three. One player from each pot was then allocated to a group. Grand Slam of Darts groups, order of play & results Afternoon sessions start at 13:00 GMT, with evening sessions at 19:00 (19:30 on 15).

But that turnover didn’t prove costly, largely thanks to Maryland’s defense, which gave the offense five drives in Wisconsin territory. The Terps were called for nine flags against Purdue, with Zion Elee’s personal foul aiding the Boilermakers potential game-winning drive. The freshman, who leads Maryland with six sacks, has committed multiple costly penalties this season. After not committing a penalty in the first four games, Elee has been flagged six times in the last six games. Three of those have been unsportsmanlike conducts along with a pair of personal fouls. The freshman has let his emotions get the best of him at points this season. “Unacceptable. First and foremost, not gonna be tolerated,” Abdul-Rahim said. “Immaturity at its best. [He] just turned 19 years old yesterday, and it’s not just him.” Elee had two of the Terps’ 11 penalties Saturday, with a roughing the kicker penalty that erased Wisconsin’s three-and-out. That prompted one of Maryland’s assistant coaches to pick up an unsportsmanlike conduct after arguing with the officials over the call. “Teachable moments are always better when you have a win behind,” Abdul-Rahim said. “So all of his teachable moments, we don’t accept that. Built on discipline.”

item.title: Mirra Andreeva sees off Jessica Pegula to reach WTA Finals showpiece
item.description: FILE PHOTO - Russian tennis player Mirra Andreeva celebrates a point against Poland's Iga Swiatek during their women's singles quarterfinal match of the Stuttgart Open tennis tournament. (is associated with: «Mirra Andreeva sees off Jessica Pegula to reach WTA Finals showpiece») Marijan Murat/dpa Mirra Andreeva stormed into the final of the WTA Finals for the first time and in the process got the last laugh over Jessica Pegula. Andreeva produced a near immaculate display in Indian Wells to win 6-3, 6-4 in 85 minutes and claim a semblance of revenge against her American rival. Pegula made headlines before the end-of-season tournament started when she made disparaging comments about Andreeva’s mentality to her coach during a training session, which were picked up on a livestream that the world number five had not been aware of. The ‘hot mic’ moment failed to stop Pegula qualifying into the semi-finals, but she had no answer to Andreeva after a shaky start. A double fault by Andreeva gifted Pegula an early break before she showed supreme mental strength to remain calm and break back with a fine crosscourt winner, and a wonderful backhand winner sealed another to move 5-3 up to help clinch set one. The second set followed a similar pattern with Pegula able to go a break up for a 3-1 lead but unable to press home her advantage, and Andreeva won five out of the final six games to reach Sunday’s showpiece without dropping a set.

item.title: Sabalenka apologises & says viral comment 'not directed at Svitolina'
item.description: Aryna Sabalenka will be replaced as world number two by Mirra Andreeva on Monday [Getty Images] Aryna Sabalenka has apologised and denied claims that she insulted opponent Elina Svitolina after a viral clip showed her swearing during her WTA Finals defeat by the Ukrainian. A video of world number two Sabalenka angrily gesturing and swearing in Russian during her 6-3 3-6 6-1 defeat by Ukraine's Svitolina was posted on social media on Saturday. Some commentators interpreted Belarusian Sabalenka's comments as an insult towards Svitolina or Ukrainians in general. Sabalenka later wrote on social media that "my comment was not directed at Elina" but she lost her temper because of the behaviour of some fans. "I was frustrated with a small group of spectators who were aggressively cheering my mistakes, and I reacted emotionally in the moment," the 28-year-old wrote. "That said, I should have handled my frustration differently, and I apologise to anyone offended." Sabalenka said Svitolina had played a great match, adding that she wished her "all the best for the rest of the tournament". Ukrainian players have a long-standing policy of not shaking hands with Russian or Belarusian players because of the ongoing invasion of their country. item.title: Nerveless Andreeva reaches WTA Finals showpiece
item.description: Mirra Andreeva won the Indian Wells title - part of the WTA Tour - last year [Getty Images] Mirra Andreeva says she surprised herself with her nerveless performance after beating Jessica Pegula to become the youngest player for 22 years to reach the WTA Finals showpiece. French Open champion Andreeva came back from a break down in both sets to win 6-3 6-4 in Indian Wells, California. The 19-year-old Russian is the youngest finalist at the season-ending event since Maria Sharapova, who was 17 when she won the title in 2004. Victory over American Pegula ensures Andreeva will finish the year as world number two. "I did not feel one bit of pressure today, I don't know why," Andreeva told Sky Sports. "Usually I feel like on these important points or when I have to close out the match or the set I get so tight. "But for some reason today I was just playing. item.description: When Drake met Bastin: A chance family encounter at Arsenal On what some might call a divinely orchestrated day, I had what remains my most surreal experience at an Arsenal game. I can remember it as clear as daylight. It was 14 March 2019, and Arsenal were due to play French side Rennes in the Europa League round of 16. They would eventually win 3-0 to reach the quarter-finals. A chance encounter at the Emirates I was standing with an old school and college friend among hundreds of fans in the concourse, waiting to go and sit down for the match. I couldn’t help but look at the Arsenal hat-trick heroes board, which showed every single hat-trick my great-grandad, 1930s Gunners legend Ted Drake, scored. Something inside me told me to tell the slightly older guy with ginger hair and black glasses next to me who my great-grandfather was. Well, by pure coincidence, he told me he was the great-nephew or great-great-nephew of Cliff Bastin, Arsenal’s all-time top goalscorer from the 1930s through to the late 1990s , when Ian Wright broke his record of 178 goals. I asked if he had ever met Cliff. He said he hadn’t, which was ironic considering I’d never met Ted either. My school friend looked stunned. What are the chances, eh? Out of 60,000 people, I was apparently speaking to someone with Arsenal in their DNA too! Well, that’s a moment I’ll never forget, for sure! Highbury 1935. (L-R): Wilf Copping, Cliff Bastin, Eddie Hapgood, Ted Drake, George Male. (Photo by J.A Hampton/Topical Press Agency/Getty Images) Two families with Arsenal in their DNA Drake set the English top-flight record for the most goals scored in a game when he hit seven away to Aston Villa on 14 December 1935. From his arrival in 1934 through to 1939, he was Arsenal’s top scorer every season, scoring 44 goals in the 1934/35 campaign, a tally no Arsenal striker has beaten. I was 16 at the time, and I told Cliff’s relative how much I respected what both players had achieved for the club and that I couldn’t believe the odds. I texted a family member moments later! During the 2022/23 season, while I was involved in the Emirates Stadium banner redesign project, I did meet the daughter and grandson of Eddie Hapgood, Arsenal’s 1930s captain and legendary defender. Of course, the grumblers will begin loading their chambers for Ohio State and Iowa weekends quickly enough. And if we’re honest, there were still moments of jaws dropping and muttered curses. And a couple of questionable 4th down calls on the coaching end. Just wanted to get that out of the way early as the players seemed to clean up their act early. The offense blazed through Rutgers for a pair of 90+ yard drives as well as 237 yards rushing, 103 by true freshman Jamal Rule who got a lot of them physically – which could be witnessed by Rutgers defenders on the field. The defense exceeded expectations with a donut on the board as they held Rutgers to 143 total yards. Not much was expected – the Scarlet Knights started their 3rd string QB and had to return to their gametime-decision backup signal caller after QB3 was knocked out of the game. Best player and WR KJ Duff had season-ending surgery earlier in the week. With these circumstances, the Blackshirts were able to focus on shutting down the running game, and for the most part, they did. They also came up with picks the two times Rutgers threatened. Thank you Caleb Benning and Jeremiah Charles. The final was 31-0. Along with Rule, there was Anthony Colandrea running things smoothly by throwing for 188 yards and a pair of scores while rushing for 68 and another on the ground. Carter Nelson, whose name keeps popping up more and more, had a pair of grabs as well as a 40-yarder which set up another ( Correction: only one TD grab, not two ) . On the defensive side, it was Vincent Shavers covering for the injured Own Chambliss with 10 tackles. The game didn’t begin lights out. The Huskers thought they had a 3 & out, but Rutgers went and made a 4th & 1 from their own 34. They picked up a few more yards before burying Nebraska on their 5 when Jacory Barney opted to fair catch one there. No problem as – check that, a familiar problem when they took a false start on their second play. But Nebraska began marching ripping off chunks of 15 and 18 yards by Rule and Colandrea respectively. Colandrea then hit Barney for a 38-yard TD pass…except the review showed he dropped it. In this case, no problem, the Huskers kept driving and Colandrea found Luke Lindenmeyer for 15 yards on a 3rd & 9, and he rumbled in for the game’s opening score. The Huskers’ second drive was fouled with a pair of pre-snap penalties after beginning when Barney fielded a second straight punt on the 5 and returned it only to the 8. The third one also started deep in their own territory when a Rutgers punt found its way out of bounds at the 10 this time. However, they were on the move, again mostly by ground, until Colandrea found Carter Nelson behind the Rutgers secondary and when he was done running, the Huskers were 40 yards downfield on the Rutgers 6. Colandrea hopped in from there for the 14-0 lead and it was becoming pretty obvious this was a mismatch. The Huskers began the 3rd quarter with a short march which found them on their 45 with a 4th and 1. “You should be able to get 1 the way you’ve been running it,” was true enough, but so was the fact it also seemed like a nice time to perhaps flip the field position battle after three straight 90+ yard drives in front of them – especially against an offense which had only managed 65 yards of 1st half offense. Things seemed a little shaky when the Knights moved to the Husker 24. Uh oh? Nope, thanks to Benning who made his pick and return. The Huskers took advantage of their first short field to roll in with Mekhi Nelson finishing things off with runs of 11 and 10 yards to go up 21-0. In between, a targeting review, after Nelson took the crown of Tariq Hayer’s helmet in his earhole, actually went Nebraska’s way! This may have been the first time a Cornhusker had actually had such a call applied to the opposition since 1897 or so. Hayer was helped off the field after the infraction, and while a lesser person might make a point of joyous karma rearing its head – but leading with its shoulder, not its helmet – I sincerely hope the injury was not serious. No way of knowing, since his ejection plus bar noise left me unable to know for sure. On their next possession, the Huskers again found themselves with a 4th down near midfield, this time at their 48. The call? Fake punt with Carter Nelson coming up short on a throw which…let’s be nice and just say it was not so great. And again, the call seemed the epitome of unnecessary – 21-point lead, lousy Rutgers offense, chance to drop them in the chum bucket with a good punt. Sigh. But it also resulted in no damage as the Blackshirts sent them packing with a 4 & out and a turnover on downs. It only took Nebraska five plays for Colandrea to hit Carter Nelson with a 13-yard TD pass for a 28-0 lead. They weren’t quite done, however. The next drive brought them far enough upfield to trot John Hohl out for a 41-yard field goal attempt. When it split the uprights, the Tiger Tom’s crowd let loose with its biggest cheer of the day. Judging by some of the laughs, a few of those cheers may have been tinged with sarcasm. Well, Notre Dame fans still believe their players carried Rudy off the field as genuine respect, despite Joe Montana saying for years they were all giggling at the joke. If they can think of that litter box of fiction as truth, then I choose to believe everyone was genuinely happy for Hohl. I know I was excited. 🌽🏈🙅🏻‍♂️ OMG, we love you John Hohl. It’s a field goal, dammit, A FIELD GOAL!!! pic.twitter.com/l3QrwFgUg7 — Corn Nation (@CornNation) November 14, 2026 Hohl’s boot gave the game its final score of 31-0 and brought on the backups. When the gun sounded, two things happened: 1) The Huskers became bowl-eligible for the 3rd straight season, the first time such a thing has happened since the Bo Pelini Era. I’m not saying that to calm those who have become so enraged this season; just pointing out a fact. 2) The Huskers notched their first shutout since the 2009 Holiday Bowl when Ndamukong Suh and the rest of the Blackshirts took out their “one more second” rage on Nick Foles and the Arizona Wildcats by the score of 33-0. This was obviously prior to their joining the Big 10 in 2011. Their last shutout in any conference play actually occurred back in 2003, a 28-0 blanking of Iowa State. As for the current Huskers, while they can’t erase the losing streak, their final games offer a chance at some redemption. Ohio State is certainly ripe for the picking after Julian Sayen went down for the season. And Iowa’s just doing Iowa things, not looking too scary very often, just hanging around and waiting for opponents to goof up and stealing that Amazon package off the porch when they look the other way. It’s a low-ceiling, high-floor approach which seems to satisfy their pasty denizens and teams. Nebraska, despite the rough start today, brought the penalties down, minus 25 yards of them back-to-back in garbage time. But if they can’t clean those up more – plus a few more areas – that Hawkeye approach certainly seems like a good way to win their fourth straight against the Huskers as well as 11 of the last 12 on Black Friday. But first, the Buckeyes. And a final chance to take down a big program finding themselves in a down year. Can they finally grab it? Stay tuned. x

item.title: Soroka Fits Houston’s Needs, Skubal A Fit for Everyone
item.description: Aug 22, 2026; Phoenix, Arizona, USA; Arizona Diamondbacks pitcher Michael Soroka (34) throws against the Cincinnati Reds in the fourth inning at Chase Field. Mandatory Credit: Anna Carrington-Imagn Images The Houston Astros face a real problem at Daikin Park. The stadium is not kind to pitchers, especially those who struggle with right-handed hitters. In 2026, the park had a home run factor of 113, which is very high by Sports Illustrated’s standards . Right-handed batters hit even more homers there, with a factor of 117. The left-field porch is only 315 feet, making it easy for power hitters to clear the fence. Houston pitchers allowed 204 home runs in 2026, the second-highest total in the majors, trailing only the Athletics. That makes limiting home runs a significant priority for the Astros this offseason. The team needs a pitcher who can keep the ball on the ground or in the strike zone. Michael Soroka from the Arizona Diamondbacks looks like a smart fit for this specific need. Limiting home runs is something he has proven possible without depending on strikeouts for survival. Why Soroka Makes Sense for Houston Soroka offers a balance that other options lack . The Astros looked at Dustin May and Casey Mize, but both have shown vulnerability to home runs. Last year Clay Holmes had a 20.7% home run rate on pulled balls, which rose to 29.4% this season. May improved his numbers, but Mize’s decline is worrying, with his expected FIP rising from 6.60 to 8.45. Soroka is different. He had his best season back in 2019 with the Atlanta Braves. He posted a 2.68 ERA and a 3.85 xFIP across 29 starts. That year, he threw 174 and two-thirds innings and recorded 4.0 fWAR. He was a revelation then, and his recent recovery from injury suggests he could be that pitcher again. He does not need to strike everyone out to be effective. The Mets Need Bigger Stars While Houston might sign Soroka, the New York Mets should not settle for a mid-tier addition. The Mets are in a different league when it comes to spending. They have the cash to make a record-setting deal for a true ace like Tarik Skubal. Joel Reuter of Bleacher Report placed the Mets at the top of the list for Skubal. He noted that the front office is not afraid to spend money to win. Reuter wrote, “In terms of sheer spending power and roster need, there is no more obvious landing spot for Skubal on a record-setting, long-term deal.” The Mets have already spent big on Max Scherzer and Justin Verlander in the past. They need to keep that momentum going this winter. Skubal, a 29-year-old left-hander, posted a combined 2.72 ERA with 186 strikeouts in 158⅔ innings between Detroit and Los Angeles in 2026. After being traded to the Dodgers in August, he recorded a 2.61 ERA and 70 strikeouts in 62 innings. Skubal was traded from the Detroit Tigers in August 2026. Detroit selected Skubal in the ninth round of the 2018 MLB Draft with the 255th overall pick. His most productive year was 2025, when he had a 2.21 ERA

item.description: Eddie Jones aired a complaint about Twickenham's in-stadium experience when he appeared on BBC Radio 5 Live this week. "Being a spectator and being told when to make noise is a bit funny," said the Japan boss, objecting to a big-screen request for an increase in volume. Jones sat stony-faced in the coaching box as the message appeared again in the midst of his team's 78-15 thrashing at England's hands on Saturday. There was little for him to enjoy on his return to Twickenham, where he was head coach for seven years. But, for the rest of a capacity crowd, it was a fun one. With junior tickets on sale at £15, there was a different atmosphere from usual. The decibels were higher, the demographic was younger, the spirits a little lighter. And England brought plenty of entertainment to the party. Thirteen tries in total, with Will Joseph's five putting him in the centre of the chorus line. The 24-year-old won his only previous England cap under Jones. Back in the summer of 2022, he was a teenage apprentice taken on tour to Australia and thrust into the second Test as a last-minute replacement. His promise has taken some time to be fulfilled. He struggled for game time and fitness at Harlequins after London Irish's bankruptcy forced him to move on from his boyhood club. An auto-immune condition that cost him the hearing in his left ear was one setback at the Stoop. But, as part of a rat pack of exciting young English-qualified backs at Gloucester this season, he has been superb: a swerving, offloading, game-breaking threat either on the wing or in midfield. England deployed him out wide, to bring some of the razzle-dazzle that they lost as Immanuel Feyi-Waboso limped out of their autumn campaign. Reports from Pennyhill Park during the week had suggested Joseph was doing a fine job of replicating Feyi-Waboso's explosive elusiveness. He certainly did on Twickenham's main stage, finishing chances with the same pace and power. "He is pretty similar to Immanuel Feyi-Waboso in the way he plays his game," said former England wing Chris Ashton on BBC Radio 5 Live. "He is just so fast. The Saracens second row led England's carry and tackle standings in the comeback performance we have been waiting for since his 14-month injury lay-off ended in May. Ellis Genge was snorting fire and bruising ribs and Maro Itoje's rejuvenation after a summer off continues. In the backline, Max Ojomoh was too clever and quick for the Japanese midfield, spotting space either for himself or others. Henry Pollock, the other point of interest in a much-changed line-up, found it harder to get into the game with ball in hand, but did the dirty work in defence and at the breakdown that some have questioned. Borthwick will be waiting nervously on news from his medical room this week, with Ollie Chessum, Seb Atkinson and George Furbank hoping to return in time for the All Blacks. But a fourth win in a row, after five successive defeats, has further buoyed up his regime. "The team is really starting to play well," he told BBC 5 Live. "It kills me that Will Joseph, I gave him his first cap, he scores five tries against me. Now that's not being very loyal, is it?," he joked. "He's a great kid. The Seattle Seahawks are elevating veteran cornerback Trevon Diggs and offensive tackle Bobby Hart from the practice squad ahead of their Week 10 matchup against the Las Vegas Raiders . As the Seahawks (5-4) prepare to visit Fernando Mendoza and the Raiders (4-5) on Sunday at 1:05 p.m. PT on CBS, Diggs will have another opportunity to contribute to Seattle’s secondary. His 20 interceptions from 2020 through 2025 were tied for the second-most in the league over that span. The Seahawks have experienced an uneven start to their Super Bowl title defense but enter Sunday’s contest with an opportunity to build momentum. Elevating Diggs gives Seattle another experienced option in the secondary before the team enters its Week 11 break. item.title: 'Painful' defeat for Republic of Ireland in Austria
item.description: Hallgrimsson's side sit third in Group B3 before their final game [Getty Images] Republic of Ireland boss Heimir Hallgrimsson said their 1-0 defeat by Austria in their penultimate Nations League game was "painful". Substitute Sasa Kalajdzic poked home the winner in Linz, with the narrow victory ensuring Austria claimed top spot and automatic promotion to League A. Chiedozie Ogbene squandered a late chance to equalise and Hallgrimsson was frustrated that they left the Raiffeisen Arena empty-handed when they had chances to secure the win which would have kept their hopes of winning the group alive. "It was painful not to get anything from this match. I think we deserved at least a draw, but we needed the win for this game to count," he told RTE. "I think we had the chances, the openings and the positions to do that, but this was not our day in goal-scoring, so it is disappointing. "Everything that we asked the players to do, they did and I think they gave everything. "For that reason, we should be happy in a way but, obviously, we don't want to be building something, we want to win games." Austria seal top spot with win over Republic of Ireland 'It is all down to details' Saturday's defeat left Hallgrimsson's side third in Group B3, a point behind Kosovo, who they face in their final game in Dublin on Tuesday. Hallgrimsson was left to rue Republic of Ireland's inability to clear the corner that Kalajdzic scored from. "We actually did have a lot of chances from that second ball in the box but it kind of never fell for our players in a good position," he added. "They have a corner that they score from on the second or third touch. "That's the game at this level. You need to be switched on and focused every second of the game." Picking up a second win in the group against Kosovo would secure a second-place finish in the group which brings with it a promotion play-off and a move up to pot two for next month's Euro 2028 qualifying draw. The Irish fell to a 1-0 defeat in Pristina in September and Hallgrimsson needs his side to finish strongly at home and pick up a vital three points. "It was always that [Kosovo] game that was more important, but we were just so close to winning this one and being able to win the group but this is football at this level, it is all down to details."

item.title: Clark quarterback Rocky Orozco voted Express-News Athlete of the Week
item.description: Clark Cougars Rocky Orozco (9) throws a pass In the second half on Thursday, Oct.29, 2026 at Farris Stadium. Brandeis defeated Clark 56-29. (Ronald Cortes) Clark junior quarterback Rocky Orozco had a career day in the Cougars' regular-season finale. Orozco threw for 453 yards and five touchdowns on 25-of-40 passing as Clark put up a valiant effort but fell to Reagan in a 55-45 shootout to end the Cougars' season. Following up his stellar day throwing the football, he has now been voted the Express-News Athlete of the Week. He was named Offensive Player of the Week on Monday and beat out four fellow finalists in the Athlete of the Week poll. Medina Valley senior Slate Crisp, the Defensive Player of the Week, made 14 tackles, including two for losses, to headline a stellar defensive as the Panthers shut out South San 42-0 and secured an undefeated regular season and District 14-5A-I title. Alamo Heights junior running back William Bishop caught six passes for 105 yards and a touchdown in the Mules' 42-11 win over Liberty Hill Legacy Ranch, and he added 16 carries for 171 yards. Davenport senior Dakota Hart was named Volleyball Player of the Week. The senior libero combined for 45 digs in playoff sweeps against Marble Falls and La Vernia. She had 30 digs against the Bears to help the Wolves reach the state quarterfinals for the fourth straight season. New Braunfels senior Shaylie Schaefer combined for 28 kills and four blocks in a pair of playoff victories over Victoria West and Burbank to help the Unicorns advance to the state quarterfinals. item.title: Portugal did the extraordinary with Cristiano Ronaldo. Can they do it without him?

For 23 years, Cristiano Ronaldo has been more than the country’s greatest footballer; he has been its defining sporting figure, a symbol of national pride and constant presence in the lives of supporters. After 234 appearances and 146 goals, the No 7 brought that chapter to a close and on Saturday night the team will play their first game without him . The national side are losing more than a great footballer; they are also losing one of the world’s biggest brands. Daniel Sá, the executive director of the Portuguese institute of marketing administration, believes Portugal require reinvention to attract at least some of the millions of viewers who tuned in because of CR7. item.title: Football Daily | Taking a brief minute to remember Pierre Sage’s impact at Crystal Palace
item.description: Sign up now! Sign up now! Sign up now? Sign up now! So farewell then, Pierre Sage . Many coaches leave under a cloud, not many have their departures completely obscured by the foul, retch-inducing one emanating from another team’s managerial circus, but such was Sage’s fate . The news section of Crystal Palace’s website helpfully tells you the amount of time it might take you to read each story it links through to. For example it should take four minutes or so to get through Tuesday’s “On this day: five big Crystal Palace birthdays”. “England: I love a knee slide!” will take you five. “Prize draw: be a mascot for our next [Bigger Vase] tie!” is a two-minute job. The statement informing the world of Sage’s exit? One minute. Eighty-three words. By way of illustration, the word “words” was the 84th of this paragraph. Just because the man’s French doesn’t mean his exit should be marked with a shrug. As I have been away at a conference, giving a presentation that the MC described as ‘sobering’, I’ve missed the last few days of football, so I was very sad to read about the passing of the great Danny Kelly . Others are far better placed to give tributes to the great man, but for younger generations who can’t comprehend the football cultural significance, Baker and Kelly represented the peak of football phone-ins. Before it became people ranting and raving about wanting the manager sacked as they’ve lost a few games or wanting the club to spend another few hundred million pounds on yet more players, it was about football supporters and supporting, from fans who actually went to games. Their peak was on BBC Radio in the 1990s, and there are too many examples of their greatness, but if I had to pick one, just one to illustrate it, it would, of course, be Gordon the Dundee United supporter and his bow tie . Rest in Peace, Danny Kelly. You gave us such joy” – Noble Francis. As they no longer seem to be ‘Dr Tottenham’, I was wondering if they had maybe passed the soubriquet on. item.title: The beautiful game: revived art prize gives football its creative due once more | Emma John
item.description: Football and the art world have long remained distant but the breadth of entries for this year’s award reveals a healthy revival It may be the Beautiful Game, but in its early decades football was a rare subject for artists. The Italian Futurist Umberto Boccioni whirled an athlete’s body into a vortex of movement in his 1913 painting Dynamism of a Soccer Player . You can see one of the earliest fine art depictions of a match – a smoggy, factory-adjactent scene called Any Wintry Afternoon in England – at the Manchester Art Gallery. If 1930s abstraction is more your thing, you can enjoy decoding the geometric shapes in Kazimir Malevich’s Painterly Realism of a Football Player – Color Masses in the 4th Dimension. I’m guessing the small green pea shape is a ball. These, in any case, were exceptions. In 1953 the Football Assocition launched an art prize, backed by the newly formed Arts Council: the winning works included Going To The Match by LS Lowry, with its crowds flocking to Bolton Wanderers’ then home ground, Burnden Park. An exhibition of the submissions, Football and The Fine Arts, toured the country and the Football Association secretary, Sir Stanley Rous, said he hoped it would finally break the barrier between those two worlds. item.title: Manchester City’s weaknesses under Enzo Maresca are being exposed
item.description: After three straight defeats, City’s manager says he will use the international break to reassess. Their problems may go beyond tactics Sign up for our free newsletter here Enzo Maresca seemed, if not quite baffled by his side’s Saturday defeat to Nottingham Forest, then at least a little put out. After seven straight wins from the start of the season, that’s now three straight defeats, a pattern so unusual that it’s been recorded only once before in top-flight English history, by Sheffield Wednesday in 1904-05. The three defeats were all different, Maresca said, although in all of them City had had more possession and more chances. In the 2-1 defeat at Aston Villa two weeks ago, City had 63% of the ball and had 15 chances to Villa’s eight. In the 1-0 home defeat to Brighton last weekend, they had 62% possession and 21 chances to seven. At the City Ground, it was 79% possession and 12 chances to 11. So Maresca is right in one way: City could look at basic statistics and say they had been unfortunate – although Forest could equally point to the fact that they went into that game third top of the expected goals table but second-bottom of the actual table. item.description: Roma and Lazio have both made unbeaten starts to the Serie A season, giving those in the Italian capital dreams of a Scudetto After nine games in 28 days, Gian Piero Gasperini finally got a moment to pause and reflect on Sunday night. The Roma manager was back in Liguria, where he worked for the best part of a decade across two stints at Genoa, to collect an award from Stelle Nello Sport – an association formed to promote sport in the region – celebrating his career achievements and commitment to courageous attacking football. The timing worked out well. Gasperini’s Roma thumped Sassuolo 3-0 on Saturday, bouncing back from a midweek defeat against Manchester United . That result meant the Giallorossi had scored 31 times in 11 Serie A games. In the past 65 years only two Italian teams – the Juventus and Napoli sides of 2017-18 – had made a more prolific start to a top-flight campaign. More importantly, Roma’s victory meant they remained undefeated in domestic competition this season. Just like their neighbours Lazio, who drew 1-1 away against Napoli in the early kick-off on Sunday. Continue reading...

item.title: Football comes together across Spain to honour Jesús de Miguel: ‘We’ve seen how fragile life is’
item.description: Across La Liga and beyond this weekend, footballers took to the field knowing it could have been them In the final few minutes before stepping into the arena once more, heading out for his 199th Osasuna match on Saturday evening, the man who has scored more first division goals than anyone in their history stopped his teammates for a moment and told them what it meant to wear the shirt. “This is very important,” Ante Budimir began as the dressing room, their sanctuary, fell silent around him. “We don’t have this shirt today for the sake of it. He was not chosen, and nor are we. It could have happened to anyone, anyone. Let us go knowing that we’re grateful to be on the pitch: playing, watching, warming up, sitting on the bench, whatever it may be. Boys, we were not chosen: not us, not him. Let us go, gratefully. Without thought. We have a grand day before us.” With that, Osasuna’s players turned left out of the room, where they were joined in the tunnel by footballers from Athletic Club, rivals from the north, and together they went out past the little shrine of Saint Fermin on to the field. They carried white lilies and all wore the same white shirts with a No 9 on the back, a black ribbon and the name of Jesús de Miguel, the Tenerife striker who died after a collision on the pitch five days earlier at the age of 30. At almost exactly the same time, 2,000km away to the west, Tenerife’s squad were walking out at the Heliodoro Rodríguez López in Santa Cruz. They did not have anyone alongside them, wore black suits not white shirts and did not have a game to play either, not this week. Continue reading...

item.description: Delap’s talents resurface in style, Gómez delights Brighton with more fireworks, and hair-pulling confusion at Everton It would have been very easy for Oliver Glasner to lose patience with Liam Delap. The forward is still only 23, yet the days when he was rattling in 12 in a Premier League season for Ipswich have come to seem a very long time ago (and his six games for Manchester City even longer). A season at Chelsea had left him bereft of confidence, an odd mix of diffidence and overaggression, devoid of composure in the box, arms flailing like a broken windmill. But the old gifts have not left him. Both goals on Saturday were the result of great muscular surges and if the first finish seemed essentially about hitting the ball as hard as possible on target, the second was a precise – and still powerful – finish in off the far post. After games such as this it’s possible to imagine him as England’s long-term replacement for Harry Kane. item.title: Rise of the ‘schooligans’: how a wave of antisocial behaviour threatens non-league football
item.description: Teenage ultras are increasingly causing disorder and communities fear it will not be long before it becomes something more dangerous It is five past three on Saturday afternoon and the teenage ultras of Hednesford Town are running late. They have arrived in Chester for their team’s National League North fixture and have hailed taxis, determined to make their presence felt at the ground. But word appears to have got out about their arrival. As one car turns away from the city’s charming half-timbered houses and into narrow residential streets, half a dozen local youths appear, haring round the corner in balaclavas. They try to attack the cab and chase after it as it pulls away. The smell of pyro is everywhere. As the taxi finally gets clear, the Chester gang stops in the middle of the road, shouting and gesticulating. One lad, no older than 16, pulls a long blade from inside his trousers and brandishes it. The incident ended there and no one was hurt, though a police investigation has been launched. The match went off without trouble too and the Hednesford gang – known at home as the “schooligans” – were escorted safely back to the station by Cheshire police. It was just another weekend in English non-league football, where a wave of antisocial behaviour is causing concern and leading the UK Football Policing Unit (UKFPU) to declare it its “most important” priority. As the disorder continues, a question remains: how long will it be before teenage trouble-making becomes something more dangerous? Continue reading...

item.title: Billions in revenue proves Fifa right on the World Cup – but only on things it cares about
item.description: The 2026 edition of the tournament brought in untold amounts of money to Gianni Infantino’s governing body The total hasn’t entirely stopped rising yet, still clicking away towards a final tally. Still, Fifa has already announced that it surpassed its own lofty revenue projections for the 2026 World Cup, bringing in $15bn, significantly more than anticipated. It appears that a third of that total – $5bn – came from ticket sales and hospitality alone, per reporting from the Times . That would mean direct income from the matchgoing fans came in five times as high in the United States, Canada and Mexico as it did at the last World Cup, in Qatar in 2022, when the total stood at $929m. While 2026’s expanded World Cup added 40 games to the schedule, the takings nevertheless went from an average of about $14.5m per match to about $48m. Continue reading...

item.title: Mourinho’s plan comes together as Real Madrid relaunch with clásico statement | Sid Lowe
item.description: It was just like old times as José Mourinho ended a night at Camp Nou with a knee slide and three points José Mourinho had already done the por qu é? , the printout and the press conference no-show in under 100 days. Now he’s done a knee slide too, and in the perfect place: back where it all began and where it can all begin again. When Kylian Mbappé scored the first in the clásico on Sunday night, Real Madrid’s manager hardly moved, sitting in the shadow of the bench – but when the striker got the second to win it with time running out, that was different. Mourinho leapt into the light, throwing himself to the grass, the knees of a 63-year-old’s trousers muddy as a schoolboy’s, stuck his tongue out and pumped his fists. He does so love it when a plan comes together. To the right of him, the bench was emptying, subs joining the players in sprinting towards the south-west corner. As they leapt about, dodging the bottles thrown towards them from the end, way, way up in the furthest corner and stuck inside a glass box like a bunch of David Blaines, the small group of Madrid fans who had come were going mad. In the main stand, a thousand phones were raised. And 600 kilometres west, back in Boadilla, Thibaut Courtois was watching his teammates from the sofa at home, presumably wrapped in a blanket and cradling a cup of Lemsip. On the morning of the biggest game there is, he awoke with flu, forced to miss out. Continue reading...

In the main stand, a thousand phones were raised. And 600 kilometres west, back in Boadilla, Thibaut Courtois was watching his teammates from the sofa at home, presumably wrapped in a blanket and cradling a cup of Lemsip. On the morning of the biggest game there is, he awoke with flu, forced to miss out. Continue reading...

item.title: Next Generation 2021: why slow and steady sometimes wins the race
item.description: Our NextGen picks from five years ago show that breaking through early does not guarantee longevity or future success Read the full updates on our class of 2021 here and here In 2021, as every year, we picked 80 players from around the world who had a chance of making it in world football – 20 from the Premier League and 60 from the rest of the world – as part of our Next Generation series . We then follow these talented boys on their journeys for five years. Often it is almost impossible to predict how they will get on (OK, when Sid Lowe sent over Lamine Yamal in 2024 we had an inkling he might do well). The ball-playing central midfielder comes from a footballing family and academy staff believe his tactical awareness is born from growing up around the game. His father, Adam, played for Brighton and is now manager along the coast at Worthing FC, while Martin (his great uncle), Paul (his grandad), and Wally (his great grandad), all enjoyed careers as players. The youngest to play in the Bundesliga at 16 years and one day, youngest player to appear in the Champions League 17 days later, youngest goal scorer in Bundesliga 11 days after that and youngest player and youngest goal scorer for the Germany Under-21 team before he has turned 17. item.title: Ousmane Dembélé quietly becomes the main man after long journey to the top
item.description: The Frenchman, who has been named the best male footballer in the world by the Guardian, has benefitted from PSG’s focus on the team rather than individuals What makes a good player great, and a great player the best? This question has been occupying me since 2014, when the Guardian first asked me to contribute to its inaugural Next Generation feature . My job was to look for a France-based talent born in 1997 who could go on to have a stellar career. After a great deal of research, I narrowed it down from my shortlist of five by asking questions not about the players’ football ability, but about other attributes: resilience, adaptability, decision-making, creativity, work ethic, response to feedback and willingness to learn. Qualities we cannot see, and are harder to measure. Continue reading...
